Q: How do content hashes, source revisions and pipeline versions define reprocessing identity?
A:
A content hash identifies particular bytes under a chosen algorithm, while a source revision identifies a source-defined update. A pipeline version identifies extraction, normalization, chunking and representation behavior.

Unchanged bytes can require reprocessing after a pipeline change; changed source metadata can matter even when text bytes remain equal. Store these identities separately and build deterministic derived keys from the required contract. A checksum is not a permission policy, and in-process hash values are not durable content digests.
Why: An unchanged PDF processed by a corrected table extractor can produce different evidence. Skipping it solely because the file digest is unchanged preserves the original extraction error.
Risk: A cache keyed only by source bytes can retain obsolete derived representations.
Trade: Fine-grained versioning avoids unnecessary work while preserving correct invalidation.
Try: Define when source, extractor, chunker and embedding changes invalidate existing artifacts.
